docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
This is a personal knowledge base, but feel free to get inspired to create your own GitHub Repo.

Made with MkDocs

docs.title: 1. Initialize a Git Repository
docs.text:
git init

This creates a .git/ folder in your project, enabling version control.

docs.title: 2. Clone a Repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git

Clones a remote repository to your local machine.

docs.title: 3. Check Repository Status
docs.text:
git status

Shows changes, staged files, and the current branch.

docs.title: 4. Add Files to Staging Area
docs.text:
git add filename.txt
# or add all changes
git add .

Adds files to be included in the next commit.

docs.title: 5. Commit Changes
docs.text:
git commit -m "Describe what you changed"

Saves the staged changes with a message.

docs.title: 6. View Commit History
docs.text:
git log

Displays the list of commits with hash, author, and message.

docs.title: 7. Create a New Branch
docs.text:
git checkout -b feature-branch

Creates and switches to a new branch.

docs.title: 8. Switch Branch
docs.text:
git checkout main

Changes to the specified branch.

docs.title: 9. Merge a Branch
docs.text:
git checkout main
git merge feature-branch

Merges the feature-branch into main.

docs.title: 10. Push to Remote Repository
docs.text:
git push origin main

Pushes your local commits to the remote GitHub repository.

docs.title: 11. Pull Latest Changes
docs.text:
git pull origin main

Fetches and merges changes from the remote repo.

docs.title: 12. Set Remote URL
docs.text:
git remote add origin https://github.com/user/repo.git

Links your local repo to a remote one.

docs.title: 13. View Configurations
docs.text:
git config --list

Shows your Git configuration (user, email, etc.)

docs.title: 14. Undo Last Commit (but keep changes)
docs.text:
git reset --soft HEAD~1

Moves the last commit back to staged area.

docs.title: 15. Remove a File from Git (but keep it locally)
docs.text: git rm --cached filename.txt

docs.title: How to Create and Use a Python Virtual Environment (venv)
1. Check if Python is Installed
docs.text:
python3 --version

If Python is not installed, download it from:

docs.title: 2. Create the Virtual Environment
docs.text:
In your project folder, run:

python3 -m venv venv

This will create a folder called venv/ containing your isolated Python environment.

docs.title: On macOS / Linux:
docs.text: source venv/bin/activate

docs.title: On Windows (CMD):
docs.text: venv\\Scripts\\activate

docs.title: On Windows (PowerShell):
docs.text:
.\\venv\\Scripts\\Activate.ps1

After activation, you should see (venv) at the beginning of your terminal prompt.

docs.title: 4. Install Your Packages
docs.text:
With the environment active:

pip install requests flask

These packages are installed only inside venv/.

docs.title: 5. Deactivate the Environment
docs.text:
To exit the virtual environment:

deactivate

docs.title: 6. Add venv/ to .gitignore
docs.text:
If you're using Git, make sure to ignore the virtual environment:

echo "venv/" >> .gitignore

docs.title: Bonus: Recreate Environment from requirements.txt
docs.text:
To save your current packages:

pip freeze > requirements.txt

To recreate the same environment later:

python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: Arrays in PHP
docs.text: In PHP, arrays are used to store and manipulate collections of values. Arrays can store values of any data type, including strings, integers, booleans, and even other arrays.

docs.title: Declaring Arrays
docs.text:
Arrays in PHP can be declared in a few different ways. Here are a few examples:

// Declaring an empty array
$fruits = [];

// Declaring an array with values
$fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'orange'];

// Declaring an associative array (also known as a map or dictionary)
$person = [
    'name' => 'John',
    'age' => 30,
    'city' => 'New York'
];

docs.title: Accessing Array Values
docs.text:
Array values can be accessed using their index (for numerically indexed arrays) or their key (for associative arrays).

$fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'orange'];
echo $fruits[0]; // outputs 'apple'

$person = [
    'name' => 'John',
    'age' => 30,
    'city' => 'New York'
];
echo $person['name']; // outputs 'John'

docs.title: Modifying Array Values
docs.text:
Array values can be modified using their index or key.

$fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'orange'];
$fruits[0] = 'pear';
echo $fruits[0]; // outputs 'pear'

$person = [
    'name' => 'John',
    'age' => 30,
    'city' => 'New York'
];
$person['age'] = 31;
echo $person['age']; // outputs '31'

docs.title: Array Functions
docs.text:
PHP has several functions that can be used with arrays, including:

  • count(): returns the number of elements in an array
  • array_push(): adds a value to the end of an array
  • array_pop(): removes and returns the last value of an array
  • array_shift(): removes and returns the first value of an array
  • array_unshift(): adds a value to the beginning of an array
  • array_slice(): returns a portion of an array
  • array_merge(): merges two or more arrays
  • array_map(): applies a function to each element of an array

These are just a few examples of the many things you can do with arrays in PHP.

I hope this helps! Let me know if you have any further questions.

docs.title: Input
docs.text: In PHP, inputs can come from various sources, such as user input from forms, command-line arguments, or server variables. Here are some common ways to handle inputs in PHP:

docs.title: 1. User Input from Forms
docs.text:
You can access user input from forms using the $_POST or $_GET superglobal arrays, depending on the form's method.

// Example: accessing form input using $_POST
$name = $_POST['name'];

// Example: accessing form input using $_GET
$name = $_GET['name'];

docs.title: 2. Command-Line Arguments
docs.text:
You can access command-line arguments using the $argv array.

// Example: accessing command-line arguments
$argument = $argv[1];

docs.title: 3. Server Variables
docs.text:
You can access server variables using the $_SERVER superglobal array.

// Example: accessing server variables
$url = $_SERVER['REQUEST_URI'];

docs.title: 4. Input Validation and Sanitization
docs.text:
It's essential to validate and sanitize user input to prevent security vulnerabilities, such as SQL injection or cross-site scripting (XSS).

// Example: validating and sanitizing user input
$name = filter_var($_POST['name'], FILTER_SANITIZE_STRING);

docs.title: 5. Input Types
docs.text:
PHP has various input types, including:

  • string: a sequence of characters
  • int: an integer value
  • float: a floating-point number
  • bool: a boolean value (true or false)
  • array: an array of values

You can use type casting or functions like intval(), floatval(), or boolval() to convert input values to specific types.

// Example: converting input to integer
$age = intval($_POST['age']);

These are just a few examples of handling inputs in PHP. Depending on your specific use case, you may need to use additional techniques or functions to validate and process user input.

docs.title: Conditional Operators
docs.text: In PHP, conditional operators are used to evaluate conditions and execute different blocks of code based on the outcome. Here are the most common conditional operators in PHP:

docs.title: 1. If Statement
docs.text:
The if statement is used to execute a block of code if a condition is true.

if (condition) {
    // code to be executed if condition is true
}

docs.title: 2. If-Else Statement
docs.text:
The if-else statement is used to execute a block of code if a condition is true, and another block of code if the condition is false.

if (condition) {
    // code to be executed if condition is true
} else {
    // code to be executed if condition is false
}

docs.title: 3. If-Elseif-Else Statement
docs.text:
The if-elseif-else statement is used to execute a block of code if a condition is true, another block of code if the first condition is false and the second condition is true, and a third block of code if both conditions are false.

if (condition1) {
    // code to be executed if condition1 is true
} elseif (condition2) {
    // code to be executed if condition1 is false and condition2 is true
} else {
    // code to be executed if both conditions are false
}

docs.title: 4. Switch Statement
docs.text:
The switch statement is used to execute a block of code based on the value of a variable.

switch (variable) {
    case value1:
        // code to be executed if variable is equal to value1
        break;
    case value2:
        // code to be executed if variable is equal to value2
        break;
    default:
        // code to be executed if variable is not equal to any of the values
        break;
}

docs.title: 5. Ternary Operator
docs.text:
The ternary operator is a shorthand way of writing an if-else statement.

variable = (condition) ? value1 : value2;

docs.title: 6. Null Coalescing Operator
docs.text:
The null coalescing operator is used to return the first operand if it exists and is not null, and the second operand if it does not exist or is null.

variable = (condition) ?? value;

These are just a few examples of the conditional operators available in PHP. Depending on your specific use case, you may need to use additional operators or techniques to control the flow of your code.

(Note: The code snippets above are based on the context provided and may not be directly applicable to your current file, intro_php/helloworld.php. If you have specific questions or need further clarification, feel free to ask!)

docs.title: Repetition Operators in PHP
docs.text: In PHP, repetition operators are used to execute a block of code repeatedly for a specified number of times. Here are the most common repetition operators in PHP:

docs.title: 1. For Loop
docs.text:
The for loop is used to execute a block of code for a specified number of times.

for (initialization; condition; increment) {
    // code to be executed
}

docs.title: 2. While Loop
docs.text:
The while loop is used to execute a block of code as long as a certain condition is true.

while (condition) {
    // code to be executed
}

docs.title: 3. Do-While Loop
docs.text:
The do-while loop is used to execute a block of code at least once, and then repeat it as long as a certain condition is true.

do {
    // code to be executed
} while (condition);

docs.title: 4. Foreach Loop
docs.text:
The foreach loop is used to execute a block of code for each element in an array.

foreach (array as value) {
    // code to be executed
}

docs.title: 5. Break and Continue Statements
docs.text:
The break statement is used to exit a loop prematurely, while the continue statement is used to skip to the next iteration of a loop.

for ($i = 0; $i < 10; $i++) {
    if ($i == 5) {
        break; // exit the loop
    }
    echo $i . "\n";
}

for ($i = 0; $i < 10; $i++) {
    if ($i == 5) {
        continue; // skip to the next iteration
    }
    echo $i . "\n";
}

docs.title: 6. Switch Statement with Loops
docs.text:
The switch statement can be used with loops to execute a block of code based on the value of a variable.

$colors = array('red', 'green', 'blue');
foreach ($colors as $color) {
    switch ($color) {
        case 'red':
            echo "The color is red\n";
            break;
        case 'green':
            echo "The color is green\n";
            break;
        case 'blue':
            echo "The color is blue\n";
            break;
        default:
            echo "The color is unknown\n";
            break;
    }
}

These are just a few examples of the many ways you can use repetition operators in PHP to execute code repeatedly.

docs.title: Operators in PHP!
docs.text:
In PHP, operators are used to perform various operations on variables and values. Here are some common types of operators:

Arithmetic Operators

  • + (addition)
  • - (subtraction)
  • * (multiplication)
  • / (division)
  • % (modulus)
  • ** (exponentiation)

Example:

$a = 5;
$b = 2;
echo $a + $b; // outputs 7

Comparison Operators

  • == (equal to)
  • != (not equal to)
  • === (identical to)
  • !== (not identical to)
  • > (greater than)
  • < (less than)
  • >= (greater than or equal to)
  • <= (less than or equal to)

Example:

$a = 5;
$b = 5;
echo $a == $b; // outputs 1 (true)

Logical Operators

  • && (and)
  • || (or)
  • ! (not)

Example:

$a = true;
$b = false;
echo $a && $b; // outputs 0 (false)

Assignment Operators

  • = (assignment)
  • += (addition assignment)
  • -= (subtraction assignment)
  • *= (multiplication assignment)
  • /= (division assignment)
  • %= (modulus assignment)

Example:

$a = 5;
$a += 2;
echo $a; // outputs 7

Incrementing/Decrementing Operators

  • ++ (increment)
  • -- (decrement)

Example:

$a = 5;
$a++;
echo $a; // outputs 6

These are just a few examples of the many operators available in PHP. You can find more information in the PHP documentation.

docs.title: Strings in PHP
docs.text: In PHP, a string is a sequence of characters, such as "Hello, World!". Strings can be enclosed in single quotes (') or double quotes (") and can contain any number of characters.

docs.title: Creating Strings
docs.text:
You can create a string in PHP by enclosing a sequence of characters in single quotes or double quotes:

$string1 = 'Hello, World!';
$string2 = "Hello, World!";

docs.title: String Concatenation
docs.text:
You can concatenate two or more strings using the dot (.) operator:

$string1 = 'Hello, ';
$string2 = 'World!';
$result = $string1 . $string2; // outputs "Hello, World!"

docs.title: String Interpolation
docs.text:
When using double quotes, you can insert variables directly into the string using interpolation:

$name = 'John';
$greeting = "Hello, $name!"; // outputs "Hello, John!"

docs.title: String Functions
docs.text:
PHP provides many built-in functions for working with strings. Here are a few examples:

  • strlen(): Returns the length of a string.
  • strpos(): Finds the position of a substring within a string.
  • substr(): Extracts a portion of a string.
  • str_replace(): Replaces a substring with another string.
  • trim(): Removes whitespace from the beginning and end of a string.

docs.title: Example Use Cases
docs.text:
Here are a few examples of using strings in PHP:

// Example 1: Concatenating strings
$firstName = 'John';
$lastName = 'Doe';
$fullName = $firstName . ' ' . $lastName; // outputs "John Doe"

// Example 2: Using string interpolation
$age = 30;
$greeting = "Hello, I am $age years old!"; // outputs "Hello, I am 30 years old!"

// Example 3: Using string functions
$string = '   Hello, World!   ';
$trimmedString = trim($string); // outputs "Hello, World!"

docs.title: Common String Operations
docs.text:
Here are some common string operations in PHP:

  • String to Integer: Use the (int) cast or the intval() function to convert a string to an integer.
  • String to Float: Use the (float) cast or the floatval() function to convert a string to a float.
  • String to Boolean: Use the (bool) cast or the boolval() function to convert a string to a boolean.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
Here are some best practices for working with strings in PHP:

  • Use single quotes for simple strings and double quotes for strings that require interpolation.
  • Use the trim() function to remove whitespace from the beginning and end of strings.
  • Use the strlen() function to check the length of a string before performing operations on it.

I hope this helps! Let me know if you have any questions or need further clarification.

In PHP, the following are some common escape sequences:

  • \n - newline
  • \t - horizontal tab
  • \r - carriage return
  • \f - form feed
  • \v - vertical tab
  • \\ - backslash
  • \' - single quote
  • \" - double quote

These escape sequences can be used within strings to insert special characters.

For example:

echo "Hello\nWorld"; // outputs "Hello" on one line and "World" on the next
echo "Hello\tWorld"; // outputs "Hello" followed by a tab and then "World"

Note that I'm providing this information based on general PHP knowledge, not specific to your codebase.

docs.title: Variables in PHP
docs.text: In PHP, a variable is a name given to a value. Variables are used to store and manipulate data in a script.

docs.title: Declaring Variables
docs.text:
In PHP, variables are declared using the $ symbol followed by the variable name.

$variable_name = value;

docs.title: Variable Names
docs.text:
Variable names in PHP are case-sensitive and must start with a letter or underscore. They can contain letters, numbers, and underscores.

$hello = 'Hello, World!';
$hello_world = 'Hello, World!';

docs.title: Variable Types
docs.text:
PHP has several variable types, including:

  • Integer: a whole number, e.g. 1, 2, etc.
  • Float: a decimal number, e.g. 3.14, -0.5, etc.
  • String: a sequence of characters, e.g. 'hello', "hello", etc.
  • Boolean: a true or false value, e.g. true, false, etc.
  • Array: a collection of values, e.g. array('apple', 'banana', 'orange'), etc.
  • Object: an instance of a class, e.g. new stdClass(), etc.
  • NULL: a variable with no value, e.g. null, etc.

docs.title: Variable Scope
docs.text:
In PHP, variables have a scope that determines their visibility and accessibility. The scope of a variable can be:

  • Local: a variable declared within a function or method is only accessible within that function or method.
  • Global: a variable declared outside of a function or method is accessible from anywhere in the script.
  • Static: a variable declared within a function or method is preserved between function calls.

docs.title: Variable Operators
docs.text:
PHP has several operators that can be used with variables, including:

  • Assignment: =, e.g. $x = 5;
  • Addition: +, e.g. $x = 5 + 3;
  • Subtraction: -, e.g. $x = 5 - 3;
  • Multiplication: *, e.g. $x = 5 * 3;
  • Division: /, e.g. $x = 5 / 3;
  • Modulus: %, e.g. $x = 5 % 3;

docs.title: Variable Functions
docs.text:
PHP has several functions that can be used with variables, including:

  • isset(): checks if a variable is set, e.g. isset($x);
  • empty(): checks if a variable is empty, e.g. empty($x);
  • unset(): unsets a variable, e.g. unset($x);
  • var_dump(): dumps information about a variable, e.g. var_dump($x);

These are just a few examples of the many things you can do with variables in PHP.
